questions: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

has_statements: In a lab psilocybin study, fewer than 1 in 20 volunteers felt strong fear.
In a Johns Hopkins psilocybin study, fewer than 5 in 100 volunteers felt strong fear.

quick_question.q: Two months after a psilocybin session, how many volunteers ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences?
quick_question.why: About 2 in 3 did, in one lab study. All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

questions: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?

lines.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
lines.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.

has_statements: In one large study, most alcohol or drug poisoning deaths after leaving prison came in the first 4 weeks.

quick_question.q: In a study of about 1.5 million people leaving prison, when was the risk of dying highest?
options: More than a year after release
quick_question.why: About 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks. With no information on drug use or tolerance, the study cannot say why.

questions: How common is using drugs alone, and why do people do it?

lines.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites said they'd used alone at least once in the past week. The most-picked reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
lines.but: It's one survey in one part of Canada, of people who already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, answered a survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

has_statements: In British Columbia in 2016 and 2017, about 7 in 10 people who died of a drug overdose were using alone.

quick_question.q: In a Canadian survey at harm reduction sites, about how many people had used drugs alone that week?
quick_question.why: About 3 in 4 had; the top reason was comfort at home. It was one survey, of people who already went to these sites.

questions: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?

lines.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year, and answered, said they'd sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.

questions: Did teen cannabis use rise after US states legalised it?

lines.short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.
lines.but: Just 7 states had surveys from both before and after the change, and only for its first few years.
how: Surveys gathered 1.4 million answers from US high school students, 1993 to 2017. Each state was compared before and after its law, against other states.
After recreational laws, the odds of past-month cannabis use were 8% lower. That is not 8 fewer teens in 100, but at most about 2.
Laws for medical cannabis, in 27 states and Washington, DC, were not linked to teen use either way, once other things were counted.
The authors suggest shops that check age make cannabis harder for teens to get. Their source: a 2012 news article. The study didn't test it.

questions: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?

lines.short: Yes, it can. In one study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine in their urine above the sports limit of the time.
lines.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, which had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.

questions: Do xylazine test strips work?

lines.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
lines.but: It's one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment, not powders or pills.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.

has_statements: Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, can also make xylazine test strips read positive.

quick_question.q: Xylazine test strips caught 37 of 38 samples with enough xylazine. With less, how many of 28?
quick_question.why: Only 6 of 28 with less xylazine read positive. The samples were residues wiped from used equipment, not powders.

questions: Does psilocybin help depression?

lines.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
lines.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.

has_statements: In a US trial, one psilocybin session with therapists lowered depression scores more than a vitamin pill did.
In a US trial, people got one psilocybin session or a vitamin pill. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin.

quick_question.q: In a 233-person psilocybin trial for hard-to-treat depression, what did the benefit look like by 12 weeks?
options: A gap that could be chance
quick_question.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between full and tiny psilocybin doses could be chance. People could probably tell what they got.

questions: Is psilocybin better than a standard antidepressant for depression?

lines.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
lines.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.

has_statements: In a trial of 59 people, psilocybin clearly beat the antidepressant escitalopram on the main depression score.
Six months after a trial, the psilocybin group was clearly less depressed than the group on the antidepressant escitalopram.

quick_question.q: Before a trial of psilocybin against the antidepressant escitalopram, what did people expect?
options: Nearly twice as much from psilocybin
quick_question.why: Nearly twice as much from psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes left no clear difference between the groups on any of six scales.

questions: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?

lines.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
lines.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.

quick_question.q: In a UK study, readers saw a made-up drug death story. Whom did they judge more harshly?
options: A man rather than a woman
A woman rather than a man
quick_question.why: Readers judged a man more harshly, and someone who took heroin rather than ecstasy; differences were small to moderate.

questions: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?

lines.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated. In a US survey, 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent about 3 years later.
lines.but: How many depends on who is counted, and in the studies we read, recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers back from Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics there, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some may still have had one or two, and treatment in between wasn't reported.

Across 21 studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, depending on how deaths and dropouts are counted. For many, the authors say, the problem is long-lasting.

For alcohol, figures for recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because studies count different groups. Many who recovered were never treated. Far fewer of everyone with a problem recover untreated in a year.

has_statements: In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent three years later.

quick_question.q: In Vietnam, 20 in 100 US soldiers reported narcotic dependence. How many did in their first year home?
quick_question.why: About 1 in 100 had been, in the year after coming home. How many had treatment was not counted.

questions: What does MDMA do to body temperature, heart and blood pressure?

lines.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: 136 healthy adults got one lab dose. The top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.

quick_question.q: People resting in a cool lab took MDMA. How many in 100 had a temperature above 38 degrees?
quick_question.why: 24 in 100 went above 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat and dancing were not tested.

questions: Does taking more MDMA raise blood levels more than you'd expect?

lines.short: Yes, it seems so: a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher, and about twice the total over the day.
lines.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
The kidneys cleared MDMA at the same pace at both doses; the rest of the body cleared it about half as fast at the larger one.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

People can feel little from an amount for several reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ. Some take more. These studies didn't test that.

questions: What side effects do cannabis medicines cause?

lines.short: More side effects than with a dummy, such as dizziness, feeling high, confusion and dry mouth.
lines.but: Short trials at the highest dose tested; long-term harms were not studied.
how: Researchers put together trials of cannabis medicines. They were compared with a dummy (placebo) or another medicine, at the highest dose each trial gave.
About 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one side effect. So did 62 in 100 on the comparison.
The odds of quitting a trial because of side effects were about three times higher, and of a serious side effect 1.4 times. Deaths did not differ.
The review gave counts out of 100 only for having any side effect, not for each one.

quick_question.q: In trials, how many people on cannabis medicines had at least one side effect?
quick_question.why: About 81 in 100, against 62 in 100 on a dummy or another medicine. Long-term harms were not studied.

questions: Do CBD products contain what their labels say?

lines.short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.
lines.but: One test of products bought online in 2016; products sold in shops, or today, may differ.
how: CBD is a substance from the cannabis plant. Researchers bought every CBD oil, tincture and vape liquid with a CBD label they found online.
A lab that did not know the labels tested them. 36 held more CBD than the label said, and 22 held less.
Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than a tenth, mostly holding more CBD than labelled.
No one took the products, and no urine was tested. So this can't say if they cause a high or a positive drug test.

questions: Does drinking at a young age lead to alcohol problems later on?

lines.short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.
lines.but: Only a few small studies followed young people over time; the big survey relied on memory.
how: In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who started drinking at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. They had to remember their first drink.
A review found only four groups of young people whose first drink was recorded as teenagers and who were followed into adulthood.
Drinking early went with more drinking problems in some of them. In others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems, were taken into account.

In US twins, the twin who drank without permission by about 15 drank more as an adult than the other twin, even in identical twins. But in identical twins it was not clearly linked to signs of an alcohol disorder.

has_statements: Starting to drink alcohol young has been shown to cause alcohol problems later in life.

quick_question.q: In a US survey, how many who first drank at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol?
quick_question.why: About 4 to 5 in 10, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. People relied on memory; cause is not known.

questions: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later?

lines.short: People who started young more often had drug or drinking problems later on.
lines.but: Studies can't show that starting young is the cause. Much of the link runs in families.
how: A 1992 US survey asked adults who had used drugs at least 12 times. About 1 in 3 who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs. For those who started at 21 or older, it was about 1 in 7.

In New Zealand, children were asked about drinking and drugs at 13 and 15, not years later. At 32, 29 in 100 of those who used several times by 15, mostly alcohol, were dependent on alcohol or drugs. For teens with similar childhoods who had not, it was 15 in 100.
In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often had drug problems by the study's rules. It was about 48 in 100, against 33 in 100 for the other twin.
A bigger twin study found the link was not strong, and much of it ran in families. Its authors think waiting longer to start would cut the risk only a little.

has_statements: Studies show that starting to drink or use drugs young is what causes drug or drinking problems later.

quick_question.q: A US survey asked adults who used drugs 12+ times. How many who started by 13 became dependent?
quick_question.why: About 1 in 3, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. Studies can't show starting young is the cause.

questions: Is ecstasy really MDMA, and how strong are the pills?

lines.short: Ecstasy pills are often MDMA, but not always, and the amount varies a lot.
lines.but: These tests end around 2002, so they may not describe pills today.
how: A 2004 review of pill tests estimated that 90 to 98 in 100 ecstasy pills held MDMA from the 1980s to the early 1990s, 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. The rest held related drugs, other things such as ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active.
The amount of MDMA in a pill ranged from none to several times more than in others, and some pills held a different drug.
People in an Australian survey thought about 1 pill in 4 or 5 was a dud.

Some people feel little from a pill, and some then take more. A weaker pill, or one with no MDMA, is one possible reason. The review did not look at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more.

quick_question.q: A 2004 review of pill tests: in the mid-1990s, how many in 100 ecstasy pills held MDMA?
quick_question.why: It was 90 to 98 earlier and nearly all by the early 2000s. Tests end around 2002, so pills today may differ.

questions: Does ecstasy damage dopamine nerve cells?

lines.short: It has not been shown that ecstasy harms dopamine nerve cells in people.
lines.but: Very little has been measured in people, so this does not show it is safe.
how: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn: the animals got a different drug.
A review found five human scan studies, and none showed a clear dopamine change.
In one, the dopamine marker was lower only in people who had also used amphetamine recently.
A by-product in spinal fluid cannot show whether nerve cells were harmed.

questions: After stopping ecstasy, do serotonin changes on scans return to normal?

lines.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
lines.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.

questions: How many deaths does alcohol cause worldwide?

lines.short: Global models estimated alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking.
lines.but: These are computer estimates built on studies of groups of people, not counted deaths.
how: The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women.
At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study: about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.
An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, mostly from injuries, heart disease, cancer and cirrhosis, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented.
A later round of the global study, quoted second-hand, put it at about 1.8 million in 2020. The numbers move with the method, so they do not show a trend.

quick_question.q: In one global study, for people aged 15 to 49, where did alcohol rank among risks for death?
options: It was not on the list
quick_question.why: At those ages it caused an estimated 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.

questions: Can drugs be ranked by how much harm they do?

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

has_statements: UK experts judged legal alcohol and tobacco less harmful than LSD and ecstasy.
In a UK expert ranking, alcohol came top mostly because of the harm it does to other people.
In a UK expert ranking, alcohol scored worse than heroin or crack for the person using it.

quick_question.q: In a UK expert ranking of harm to the person using, which drug was among the worst three?
quick_question.why: Crack cocaine, heroin and meth scored worst for the person using. Alcohol topped the overall list mostly through harm to others.

questions: What does a second dose do to the heart and body?

lines.short: Taking more adds strain on the heart and blood pressure without stronger good feelings.
lines.but: Small laboratory studies of healthy, screened people sitting in a quiet room.
how: After a second dose, 8 of 9 men went above a raised blood-pressure line, against 6 of 9.
Both cases of a racing heart in that study came after the second dose.
In another study, all ten men went above that line.
Nobody has tested hot, crowded places or the larger amounts people describe.

questions: Does MDMA stop working as well with regular use?

lines.short: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
lines.but: This comes from questionnaires, retold in one review; no laboratory study has tested it.
how: In surveys, most people say the first time was the strongest.
People who have used more say they take more tablets in a night.
Nobody checked what the tablets held, and different people were compared, not followed over time.
In one study, longer use did not go with more tablets.

questions: Does caffeine make you sharper, or just undo withdrawal?

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

has_statements: In a lab study, caffeine made people who have it often more alert than people who rarely have it.
In one study, caffeine made people who often have it more alert than people who rarely do.

quick_question.q: In a caffeine study, who quit the test day early with headache and feeling sick?
options: People who often have caffeine, on dummy pills
People who rarely have caffeine, on caffeine
People who often have caffeine, on caffeine
quick_question.why: All five people who often have caffeine and quit early had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons. One study.

questions: Do clonidine or lofexidine help with opioid withdrawal?

lines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, fewer people had bad withdrawal and more finished treatment.
lines.but: Only three small, old trials, mostly in hospital, and none with people coming off fentanyl.
how: Three trials gave people coming off heroin either the medicine or a dummy pill, picked by chance.
Bad withdrawal happened to about 19 in 100 on the medicine and about 59 in 100 on the dummy pill.
About 56 in 100 finished treatment on the medicine, against 29 in 100 on the dummy pill.
The medicine made some people sleepy or dizzy and lowered their blood pressure.

quick_question.q: In trials, how many in 100 coming off heroin had bad withdrawal on clonidine or lofexidine?
quick_question.why: About 19 in 100, against about 59 on a dummy pill. Only three small, old trials, and none with people coming off fentanyl.

questions: What happens with SSRI antidepressants?

lines.short: An SSRI muted MDMA's effects in lab tests; with paroxetine, MDMA blood levels rose.
lines.but: Only 28 healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most, and no one was given more MDMA.
how: 16 volunteers rated MDMA's effects about 60 percent lower after citalopram; their blood levels were not measured.
In 12 men, paroxetine lessened the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size. Yet the MDMA peak in the blood was about 1 in 6 higher.
Feeling little can have many reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here.
No one was given more MDMA once its effects were muted, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk.

questions: In MDMA deaths, which medicines were found too?

lines.short: Among 19 Australian deaths with MDMA and a risky mix, antidepressants, opioids and benzos were common.
lines.but: The 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the counts do not show how common any mix is.
how: In 14,682 coroners' cases (2002 to 2008), 106 had MDMA in the blood. Six in 10 of them died of injuries such as hanging or a crash, so MDMA in the blood does not show that it caused the death.
The authors rated 19 of the 106 as having a risky drug combination. Of those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine (benzo).
Four of them had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type. Three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died.

A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.

questions: MDMA with MAOI antidepressants such as moclobemide?
What about MAOI antidepressants, like moclobemide?

lines.short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.
lines.but: Four deaths cannot give a rate, and all four also had other drugs in their blood or urine.
how: None of the four had been prescribed moclobemide. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs.
The authors thought it was serotonin syndrome, but its defining signs were not recorded. MDMA levels were about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes.
Reviews rank MDMA with this kind of antidepressant as the highest-risk mix they list. Nobody has counted people who took both and had no such outcome.
Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more. No study measured what happens then with this antidepressant.

questions: Cocaine with alcohol: what happens to the heart?

lines.short: Together they make a new substance, cocaethylene, and hearts beat faster than with cocaine alone.
lines.but: Small hospital studies of 8 and 6 people. None measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.
how: Eight adults who already used both drugs took cocaine by the nose on a hospital ward. With alcohol, their heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute, against 74 with cocaine alone.
There was also about 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in their blood, and cocaethylene, which the body makes only when both drugs are there and which leaves the blood more slowly than cocaine.

In a second study, cocaine went into a vein with alcohol. Cocaethylene formed again, but stayed at a small fraction of the cocaine level, and none of it appeared when cocaine was given without alcohol.

Cocaethylene has been found in people's blood after both drugs, including after deaths, but such tests cannot show what caused a death. In over 1,000 emergency-room tests, people positive for both drugs had no more heart problems than people positive for one.

has_statements: When people use cocaine with alcohol, the body makes a new substance, cocaethylene, that forms only when both are there.

quick_question.q: In a small lab study, what happened to heart rate when alcohol was added to cocaine?
options: It was faster than with cocaine alone
It was slower than with cocaine alone
quick_question.why: Heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both drugs, against 74 with cocaine alone, in 8 people.

questions: What is meth withdrawal like, and how long does it last?

lines.short: After stopping, most symptoms people reported eased within one to two weeks. Low mood and craving lasted longer.
lines.but: It was one small study on a hospital ward. The people in it were not seeking treatment.
how: People dependent on meth stopped using on a hospital research ward.
Most symptoms they reported eased within one to two weeks.
Low mood lasted about three weeks; craving lasted to week five, at a lower level.
They were not looking for treatment. None had another mental-health diagnosis at the time.

has_statements: In one small study, most symptoms of stopping meth eased within one to two weeks.

quick_question.q: In one small study of people stopping meth, which lasted longest?
quick_question.why: Most symptoms eased in one to two weeks, low mood lasted about three, and craving lasted to week five.

questions: Do colour tests like Marquis show whether a pill has MDMA in it?

lines.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
lines.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.

quick_question.q: In one lab study, some MDMA samples also had caffeine or amphetamine. What did a colour test show?
options: The same colour as MDMA alone
quick_question.why: Seven MDMA samples with another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour. One small 2003 study, with a kit of that time.

questions: Is the day after worse with synthetic cannabis than with ordinary cannabis?

lines.short: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover.
lines.but: These are memories from a 2011 online survey; nobody tested the products.
how: About a thousand people who had used both compared them in an online survey.
They said synthetic cannabis made it harder to get on with things afterwards.
They said it gave more bad feelings and fear of others while high, and much less enjoyment.
Most preferred ordinary cannabis, and said synthetic cannabis wore off sooner.

has_statements: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover than ordinary cannabis.

quick_question.q: How did people who had used both rate synthetic cannabis against ordinary cannabis while high?
options: More bad feelings, much less enjoyment
quick_question.why: They said it gave more bad feelings and fear of others, and much less enjoyment; most preferred ordinary cannabis. Nobody tested the products.

questions: Does one dose of meth make thinking worse at the time?

lines.short: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.
lines.but: The studies were small, so small or moderate harm can't be ruled out. Binges were not tested.
how: Lab studies gave people mostly single doses.
Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse. On some tasks people did better.
The studies were small. The two main ones, and the review of the others, came from one research group.
Binges and long-term use were not tested.

quick_question.q: In small lab studies, what did a single dose of meth do to attention and memory?
quick_question.why: Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse, but the studies were small and binges were not tested.

questions: Do police believe touching fentanyl can cause overdose? Does training change that?

lines.short: In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death. Right after trainings, far fewer did.
lines.but: No survey picked people at random. Answers came right after training, with no untrained group or later check.
how: In Missouri, only about 1 in 5 of 140 police, paramedics and firefighters rejected the idea before training; about 5 in 6 did right after.
Officers in five US police forces said they heard it from colleagues, a federal drug agency video and bulletins; none could confirm a colleague's overdose.
506 of 551 US news articles were coded misinformation, even plain reports of ill officers. They got about 450,000 Facebook shares; clear corrections, under 30,000.

In a 2019 New York online survey, 149 of 187 police, fire and ambulance workers agreed a brief touch could be deadly. For fentanyl safety information, most named courses and training; about 1 in 7, the news.

has_statements: Most first responders in a New York survey said the news was their source on fentanyl.
Before a training, most first responders surveyed in Missouri thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose.

quick_question.q: A New York survey asked police, fire and ambulance workers about fentanyl. About how many agreed a brief touch could be deadly?
quick_question.why: About 4 in 5: 149 of 187. No survey picked people at random, so it may not speak for all responders.

questions: What is the cocaine crash, and how long does it last?

lines.short: After a binge, people described a crash: very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger.
lines.but: This is what some people in treatment told their doctors; it cannot show how often it happens.
how: Doctors talked with 30 people who came for help with heavy cocaine use; there was no comparison group.
The crash began soon after the last use and usually ended within a few days.
Some people had passing thoughts of suicide, which were limited to the crash.
Many had used alcohol or other drugs to get to sleep.

has_statements: People who sought help for heavy cocaine use said the crash after a binge usually ended within a few days.

quick_question.q: What did people describe in the crash after a cocaine binge?
options: Days of extra energy, little need for sleep
Very low mood, then long, heavy sleep
Feeling normal again by the next day
quick_question.why: Very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger. Some had passing thoughts of suicide, limited to the crash. From 30 people in treatment.

questions: On methadone or buprenorphine and also prescribed sedatives?

lines.short: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, benzo prescriptions were linked to more poisoning deaths.
lines.but: The study did not take mental health, alcohol or street drug use into account.
how: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people per year with a benzo prescription, and 1 in 200 without.
The link was stronger when benzo doses were above the highest dose the UK drug guide advises.
Sleeping tablets called z-drugs were also linked to poisoning deaths, though deaths were few.
People prescribed benzos stayed in treatment longer, but the link with poisoning deaths was still there.

quick_question.q: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, how many people with benzo prescriptions died of poisoning each year?
quick_question.why: About 1 in 100 a year with a benzo prescription, 1 in 200 without. The study did not allow for alcohol or street drugs.

questions: Does acamprosate help people stop drinking?

lines.short: In trials, 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 on dummy pills.
lines.but: The most carefully run trials found no clear difference.
how: Acamprosate is a tablet. Most trials were in Europe, in people who had already stopped drinking.
About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again during treatment, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills. It did not cut heavy drinking.
The most carefully run trials, including the two largest of them, both in the US, found no clear difference. Most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker.
Diarrhoea was more common: about 11 more people in every 100. In one review, more people stopped taking it because of side effects.

has_statements: The most carefully run acamprosate trials found it clearly helped people stop drinking.

quick_question.q: In acamprosate trials, how many in 100 drank again during treatment, against 83 on dummy pills?
quick_question.why: About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 on dummy pills. The most carefully run trials found no clear difference.

questions: How common are fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) and fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS)?

lines.short: About 8 in 1,000 children are thought to have FASD. About 1.5 in 1,000 people have FAS.
lines.but: Few countries had counted it. Most numbers were worked out from how many women said they drank.
how: FASD is the name for the effects of alcohol on a child before birth. It covers several diagnoses, and FAS is one of them.
Researchers found 24 studies in 8 countries that looked for FASD in children. Results ranged from under 1 to about 208 in 1,000, by place and method.

For most countries there was no count. The team took the estimated share of women who drank in pregnancy and divided it by one fixed number. In the regions with the lowest figures, no study had counted it.
That number is an average from a few countries. It is not the chance for any one pregnancy. Ways to diagnose FASD also differ.

quick_question.q: About how many children in 1,000 are thought to have FASD, the effects of alcohol before birth?
quick_question.why: About 8 in 1,000. Few countries had counted it; most numbers were worked out from how many women said they drank.

questions: Does naltrexone help people drink less?

lines.short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.
lines.but: Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.
how: Naltrexone is a tablet. Dozens of trials gave it or dummy pills, mostly for 3 months, usually with counselling as well.
About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely.
People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common.
When compared directly, naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same, but most people in that comparison were in one trial.

has_statements: Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely.

quick_question.q: In naltrexone trials, how many in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills?
quick_question.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone, against 54 on dummy pills. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped and had counselling.

questions: Do medicines prevent seizures in alcohol withdrawal?

lines.short: In old trials, benzodiazepines cut seizures: about 1 in 100, against 8 on dummy pills.
lines.but: The trials were from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.
how: Benzodiazepines are calming medicines. Old trials gave them or dummy pills to people going through alcohol withdrawal.
About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills. Delirium was also less common: about 2 in 100 against 6.
Other medicines were not clearly better or worse. One kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines.
Few trials looked at people who already had the DTs.

quick_question.q: In alcohol withdrawal, how many in 100 on benzodiazepines had a seizure, against 8 on dummy pills?
quick_question.why: About 1 in 100 on a benzodiazepine, against 8 on dummy pills. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few had seizures.

questions: Can caffeine bring on panic attacks in people with panic disorder?

lines.short: About half had a panic attack after one big dose; none after a dummy.
lines.but: Most studies used one large amount. The review cannot show what ordinary smaller servings do.
how: A 2022 review included 10 small lab studies of adults with panic disorder during a break from psychiatric medicines.
After caffeine, 121 of 237 had a panic attack. None was reported after a dummy drink or capsule, though not everyone completed both conditions.
In studies with both groups, about 54 in 100 people with panic disorder had an attack after caffeine, against 2 in 100 without it.
Anxiety also rose more after caffeine than a dummy in all five studies that tested that comparison. The pooled anxiety result was a different comparison: change after caffeine in the two groups.

quick_question.q: In lab studies, how many with panic disorder had a panic attack after one large amount of caffeine?
quick_question.why: 121 of 237 had a panic attack after caffeine; none was reported after a dummy. The review cannot show what ordinary smaller servings do.

questions: Does a CBD medicine reduce seizures in a severe childhood epilepsy?

lines.short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.
lines.but: The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result did not always hold up.
how: First trial, 120 children: seizures at least halved in 43 in 100 on CBD and 27 on the dummy liquid. That gap could be chance.
Second trial, 198 children: 44 and 49 in 100 in two CBD groups saw seizures at least halve. On the dummy liquid, 26 did.
The second report said backup checks agreed. Yet with missing diary days filled in, one CBD group no longer clearly beat the dummy liquid.
On CBD, 23 to 36 in 100 children were sleepy, against 10 to 14 on the dummy liquid. Shop CBD was not tested.

has_statements: Trials show that CBD oil from a shop cuts seizures in children with a severe epilepsy.

quick_question.q: In two trials of a CBD medicine for Dravet syndrome, how many children saw seizures at least halve?
quick_question.why: 43 to 49 in 100 on the CBD medicine, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid.

questions: What happens to your sleep when you stop using a lot of cannabis?

lines.short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.
lines.but: Three small studies, two of them from the 1970s with very strong lab doses.
how: Sleep was measured in a lab while people were still using cannabis and after they stopped.
After stopping, they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream (REM) sleep.
The pooled data came from the first week after stopping, so this review cannot say how long the changes last.

quick_question.q: In sleep-lab studies, how did sleep change in the first nights after stopping heavy cannabis use?
options: Longer sleep, quicker to start, less dream sleep
Shorter sleep, slower to start, more dream sleep
quick_question.why: They slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream sleep. Three small studies, two from the 1970s.

questions: Does cocaine narrow heart arteries, and do beta-blockers make it worse?

lines.short: Yes, in a lab cocaine narrowed heart arteries a little. After a beta-blocker, blood flow fell further in all 10 patients, but its effect on heart attacks is unknown.
lines.but: No trial has ever tested beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine.
how: That lab test used 10 heart patients who had never used cocaine. The beta-blocker, propranolol, went straight into a heart artery.
In 2008, US heart doctors advised against beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine. That rests mainly on small lab tests, animal tests and expert opinion.
In hospital records of about 2,000 people, heart attacks and deaths were not clearly different with beta-blockers. But doctors chose who got them.
Two reviews counted one cocaine study's blood tests as heart attacks or damage. That study of 58 people reported no heart complications or deaths.

has_statements: The warning against beta-blockers after cocaine is based on big trials.

quick_question.q: In a lab, what happened to heart blood flow when 10 people got the beta-blocker propranolol after cocaine?
quick_question.why: It fell in all 10 heart patients. None had used cocaine before.

questions: Do fentanyl strips pick up drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil?

lines.short: In lab tests, strips found most related drugs, but not all. Carfentanil needed large amounts.
lines.but: These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff. The largest study reported no repeat tests.
how: One lab tested 28 related drugs on four brands. At high amounts, 21 to 24 of them showed up.
At lower amounts, only 5 to 12 of the 23 tested showed up.
Three never showed up on any brand. Carfentanil showed only at high amounts, and never on one brand.
A second lab found 11 of 13 related drugs on all five batches of one brand. On two of the three newer batches, carfentanil showed only in very large amounts.

quick_question.q: In lab tests, did fentanyl strips pick up drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil?
options: Most but not all; carfentanil needed large amounts
Yes, all of them, even in tiny amounts
quick_question.why: At high amounts, 21 to 24 of 28 related drugs showed up; three never did, on any brand.

questions: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths?

lines.short: Sometimes: at one centre, about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause.
lines.but: Only two US places have been studied, so other places may differ.
how: At a North Carolina autopsy centre (2016 to 2021), 2,719 deaths were thought to be drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 10 in 100 had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs. In some, the tests found no drug at all.
It went the other way too. Of 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs, drug tests showed that about 49 in 100 were.

In Alabama, three doctors were told everything about 60 chosen deaths except what the autopsy found inside the body. Their cause of death matched the autopsy doctor's in 67 to 80 of every 100. They did not always agree with each other either.
In 2018, about 11 in 100 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug tests. Small offices had them less often than big ones.

has_statements: About 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths at one US autopsy centre had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs.

quick_question.q: At one US autopsy centre, deaths nobody thought were from drugs were tested. How many were drug deaths?
quick_question.why: Drug tests showed about 49 in 100 were drug deaths. Only two US places have been studied, so other places may differ.

questions: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs (the 'gateway' idea)?

lines.short: Not known. Cannabis usually comes first, but that does not prove it leads on.
lines.but: Shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain the cannabis link.
how: In New Zealand, at least 86 in 100 young people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before.
Australian twins grew up together. The one starting cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100.
A computer model where cannabis did nothing still made the same pattern. Some people were likelier to use any drug, and were offered cannabis first.
Experts disagreed about the New Zealand cannabis link. One said hidden factors no longer explain it away; another said factors changing with age still could.

has_statements: A computer model gave cannabis no effect at all. Yet people in it still mostly used cannabis first.

quick_question.q: In Australian twins, one started cannabis before 17. Who more often used cocaine or other stimulants?
options: The twin who started cannabis early
quick_question.why: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100. Growing up together can't explain it, but other differences between the twins could.

questions: Do the two mirror-image forms of ketamine, S and R, do different things?

lines.short: In one small study the S form caused psychosis-like effects; the R form did not.
lines.but: Only ten people took part, and everyone could tell when they had been given a drug.
how: Ten healthy people had the S form, the R form and a dummy, a month apart.
On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self.
On the R form, the same people described relaxation, and their brain scans moved the other way.
The ordinary mix of the two forms was never given to these same ten people.

quick_question.q: In one small study, what did ketamine's S form do that its R form did not?
quick_question.why: On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self; on R, they described relaxation. Only ten people.

questions: What side effects do people have from ketamine treatment for depression?

lines.short: With ketamine for depression, studies most often found headache and dizziness. Next came feeling unreal and higher blood pressure. Most soon passed.
lines.but: Only 12 of 60 studies checked again 2 weeks or more after the last dose, and just 5 checked the bladder.
how: A review of 60 studies up to 2016 listed side effects but could not say how often each happens. Most people had a single dose.
Raised blood pressure and heart rate came during or just after the drip and mostly settled within 90 minutes.
In a 7-person trial, all felt 'high' on ketamine and none on salt water. On average it was gone within 2 hours after the drip.
In a large trial, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect within 3 weeks, against 32 in 100 on ECT.

has_statements: Most of 60 studies of ketamine for depression checked the bladder.

quick_question.q: In a large trial, how many in 100 on ketamine drips had a moderate or severe side effect?
quick_question.why: 25 in 100 had one within 3 weeks of ketamine drips, against 32 in 100 on ECT.

questions: Is your thinking different the day after LSD?

lines.short: A few small changes, some better and some worse, which may just be chance.
lines.but: One study of 24 people after one small lab dose; this report gives no mood or sleep data.
how: People took LSD on one day and a dummy drink (placebo) on another, in random order.
The next morning, a few memory and word tests went a little better after LSD.
One card-sorting puzzle about switching rules went a little worse after LSD.
The researchers checked many scores without allowing for that, so some differences may be luck.

quick_question.q: The day after LSD in one lab study, how did people do on thinking tests?
options: A few small ups and downs
quick_question.why: A few tests went slightly better and one slightly worse, in 24 people after one small lab dose. Some may be luck.

questions: What side effects did MDMA cause in trials outside PTSD?

lines.short: In small trials, MDMA's side effects were common and brief, and none were serious.
lines.but: These trials were too small to show rare or later harms.
how: Five small studies gave MDMA to 58 people. They had anxiety, depression, social anxiety with autism, or PTSD in couples.
A tight jaw, thirst, sweating and headache were common during sessions. Tiredness was common in the week after.
Blood pressure, pulse and body heat went up during sessions. None of this needed treatment.
Thoughts of suicide were recorded as side effects in a few people; in one trial this was as common with the dummy pill.

quick_question.q: In small MDMA trials, what was common in the week after a session?
quick_question.why: Tiredness was common in the week after, while a tight jaw, thirst and sweating came during sessions.

questions: Is meth linked to depression?

lines.short: People who use meth report low mood somewhat more often than people who don't.
lines.but: Other differences, such as using other drugs or a hard life, may explain part of it: against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference.
how: Across 6 studies, after allowing for some other differences, the odds of low mood were about 1.3 times higher.
Most studies measured symptoms, not diagnosed depression.
Two studies that followed people over time, allowing for how they felt before, found about 1.5 to 1.6 times the odds.
Among people who use other drugs, those who used meth did not report clearly more low mood.

quick_question.q: Compared with people who use other drugs, how often do people who use meth report low mood?
quick_question.why: No clear difference. They report somewhat more low mood than people who don't use meth, but other drug use may explain part.

questions: How many people who use meth or amphetamine regularly die each year?

lines.short: Among people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
lines.but: These were people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Not all of it is the drug.
how: In studies of people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
That is nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex.
Overdose deaths were about 25 times as common; suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures are less certain.
Many also used opioids or injected, so this does not show how much is due to the drug itself.

quick_question.q: People with regular or problematic meth use died how many times as often as others their age?
quick_question.why: Nearly 7 times others of the same age and sex, about 1 in 90 a year; many also used opioids, so not all is meth.

questions: How long does meth-related psychosis last?

lines.short: In a typical study of people with meth psychosis, about 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.
lines.but: Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.
how: A review of 27 studies, mostly of hospital patients, looked at how long symptoms lasted.
In the typical study, 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.
How many were later told they had schizophrenia varied a lot between studies, from about 1 in 20 to 2 in 5. One review's average was about 1 in 5. This does not show that meth caused it.
Psychosis often comes back when people use again.

has_statements: Psychosis (losing touch with reality) linked to meth often comes back when people use again.

quick_question.q: In a typical study of meth psychosis, how many still had symptoms over a month after stopping meth?
quick_question.why: About 1 in 4 in the typical study, but single studies ranged from none to almost all, mostly in hospital patients.

questions: Is meth linked to violence?

lines.short: Two long-term studies linked meth use to more violence. This held after other things were counted.
lines.but: Both studies share authors, and neither could show which came first.
how: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became unclear once other things were counted.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth reported somewhat more violence in times they used meth or speed. This held after other things were counted.
In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth reported violent crime in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 without.
That study compared each person with themselves. But people reported use and crime for the same months.

quick_question.q: In one study, people dependent on meth reported violent crime in how many of 100 months of use?
quick_question.why: About 12, against 3 of 100 months without meth; people reported both for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

questions: Does the ADHD medicine methylphenidate cause sleep problems?

lines.short: Children on methylphenidate had sleep problems recorded more often than children on a dummy pill.
lines.but: The review says how many times more often, not how many children out of 100.
how: A review combined 35 trials in children and teenagers with ADHD.
Trouble falling asleep was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine as with the dummy pill.
Who recorded sleep problems, and whether a questionnaire was used, changed how big the difference looked.
A drug company paid for the review, and two of the authors work for its parent company.

quick_question.q: In trials, how often was trouble falling asleep recorded on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate versus a dummy pill?
quick_question.why: Nearly three times as often, though who recorded sleep problems changed how big the difference looked.

questions: Do official counts miss heroin deaths?

lines.short: In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than records did.
lines.but: Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.
how: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine. Some death records said morphine or mixed drugs instead of heroin.
In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 52 in 100 of the deaths a fuller review linked to heroin.

In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), about 34 in 100 deaths a review linked to heroin lacked the heroin code in national figures. A few deaths coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance.
In England and Wales, an estimate came out about half as large again as the official count. It mixed heroin with morphine and did not match each death.

has_statements: In Maryland, death certificates named heroin in almost every death a fuller review linked to heroin.

quick_question.q: Why can a death record say morphine when the person took heroin?
options: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine
Heroin and morphine are the same drug
quick_question.why: Heroin quickly turns into morphine in the body, so some death records said morphine instead of heroin.

questions: Can poppers damage your eyes?

lines.short: It seems so, in some people: reports describe blurry central vision and damage at the back of the eye.
lines.but: These are uncontrolled reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot prove poppers were the cause, or show how often it happens or which poppers do it.
how: Doctors in at least 12 countries have written about 113 people with eye problems after poppers, some after using them once.
Most had both eyes affected: blurry or dim vision in the middle, flashes of light, or a blank spot.
In most people scanned, the scans showed damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina, at the back of the eye.
Of the people who had a second scan, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing.

has_statements: Eye problems after poppers have only been reported after years of heavy use.

quick_question.q: In people with eye problems after poppers, what did scans mostly show?
options: A cloudy lens, like a cataract
Damage to light-sensing cells at the back
Scratches on the front of the eye
quick_question.why: Scans mostly showed damage to light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina. People reported blurry central vision, flashes or a blank spot.
